lines.statement:
In adults in a pooled analysis of six case-control studies (2,159 people with lung cancer and 2,985 controls; four of the six studies unpublished) and in Swedish male military conscripts (49,321 at the start, 44,257 in the cannabis analysis) followed for 40 years, to about age 60 (the pooled analysis as described by the National Academies committee, a narrative review, and not read here, so its figures are second-hand; the cohort from its own paper, read in full), evidence is insufficient to say whether smoking cannabis, compared with not smoking cannabis, changes the incidence of lung cancer.

In the pooled analysis, habitual cannabis smoking (at least 1 joint-year) against non-habitual (under 1 joint-year, including never) gave an odds ratio of 0.96 (95% CI 0.66–1.38), and 1.03 (0.51–2.08) among people who did not smoke tobacco; for adenocarcinoma alone the odds ratios were 1.73 (0.75–4.00) for more than 1 joint a day and 1.74 (0.85–3.56) for more than 10 joint-years, not significant. The committee says risk rose with duration and intensity without becoming significant. In the Swedish cohort (the paper itself), 'heavy' use meant reporting, once, at conscription at age 18 to 20, more than 50 uses of cannabis in a lifetime (831 men, 1.7%). These men had a hazard ratio of 2.12 (1.08–4.14) for lung cancer against men who reported never using cannabis, adjusted for tobacco smoking (in three bands: none, 1 to 10 and more than 10 cigarettes a day), alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status, each measured only at conscription; unadjusted it was 3.72 (1.96–7.06), and adjusted for tobacco alone 2.24 (1.17–4.29). Ever having used cannabis was not associated with lung cancer once tobacco was counted (1.25, 0.84–1.87, from 1.90 unadjusted), and the lower bands of use showed no rise with more use (fully adjusted, from once to 11 to 50 uses: 1.52, 0.66, 0.68 and 1.68, none significant); the authors report no clear dose–response relationship. Of the men in the heaviest band, 91% also smoked tobacco (62% more than 10 cigarettes a day, against 23% of the men who never used cannabis), and analyses within tobacco groups were unstable or could not be estimated because too few men used cannabis without tobacco: in the paper's Supplemental Table 1, the 678 men who reported using cannabis but no tobacco had one lung cancer between them (in the 216 who had used cannabis once), so no hazard ratio could be estimated for men who had used cannabis more than once without tobacco. Over follow-up from 1970 to 2009 (about 1.9 million person-years), 189 of the 49,321 men had a lung cancer record (about 4 in 1,000; 179 in the analyses); the paper gives no count by cannabis group, so absolute risks by group cannot be given. The committee says studies in an epidemiologic review that are not in the pooled analysis indicate an increased risk.

The committee graded the evidence 'moderate evidence of no statistical association' between cannabis smoking and the incidence of lung cancer (its wording and its judgment; under it sit the pooled case-control analysis and, in its discussion, the cohort and the review). The editors read 'no statistical association' here as not statistically significant in a pooled estimate whose interval does not exclude an odds ratio of 1.38 (a 38% rise) or, among people who did not smoke tobacco, of 2.08, with a cohort pointing up; it is not a finding that smoking cannabis does not raise the risk, and the chapter's highlights go further than its numbered conclusion. A 2018 commentary sets the committee's wording beside a WHO statement (the WHO report was not read) that a cannabis and tobacco mix may increase cancer risk and that the effect of cannabis alone is unknown.

Not measured and limits, as the committee names them: the pooled analysis could not account for differences in smoking technique or in the cannabis smoked, had few people with heavy long-term smoking (imprecise estimates) and relied on self-report without biological confirmation; in the cohort (confirmed in its paper), cannabis and tobacco use after conscription were not recorded, nor how cannabis was smoked, how much or how strong it was; its authors did not know whether participants mixed tobacco into their cannabis, which they say would inflate the cannabis-related risk; and the self-reports were not anonymous, which they say may have led to under-reporting, while some men may have over-reported to be exempted from military training. Follow-up ended when the men were 58 to 60 (editors' calculation from birth years 1949 to 1951), younger than the median age of about 70 at a first lung cancer diagnosis that the authors cite; lung cancers came from hospital inpatient records to 2009 and death records to 2006, not from the cancer register; and the 7.6% of men who did not answer the cannabis questions had a lower risk than men who reported never using it (0.41, 0.17–0.99). The committee adds that cancers have a long incubation period that needs long observation, that cannabis smoke, like tobacco smoke, contains carcinogens, that cannabis use has been associated with cigarette smoking (to which 28.6% of US cancer deaths in 2014 have been attributed, in a study it cites), and that replication is needed because exposures are changing and many associations rest on single studies. No source read compares smoking cannabis with other ways of taking it.

Funding as printed: the committee's report was sponsored by US federal agencies and health foundations, with no cannabis or tobacco industry sponsor listed; the cohort paper was funded by an institutional grant from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and by the Swedish Council for Working Life and Social Research, which the paper says had no role in the study, and its authors declare no conflicts of interest; the funding of the pooled analysis is not given in the committee's account and is not known here. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
lines.population: Adults in a pooled analysis of six case-control studies (2,159 people with lung cancer, 2,985 controls; four studies unpublished) and men in a Swedish cohort of military conscripts (49,321 at the start, 44,257 in the cannabis analysis) aged 18 to 20 at the start and followed 40 years, to about age 60 (pooled analysis as described by the National Academies committee; cohort from its own paper)
lines.exposure: Smoking cannabis, self-reported: habitual (at least 1 joint-year) in the pooled analysis; more than 50 lifetime uses reported once, non-anonymously, at conscription at age 18 to 20 in the Swedish cohort (use after conscription, technique, amount, product strength and any tobacco mixed in not recorded)
lines.comparator: Non-habitual cannabis smoking (under 1 joint-year, including never) in the pooled analysis, also within people who did not smoke tobacco; men who reported never using cannabis at conscription in the Swedish cohort (55% of whom smoked tobacco then)
lines.outcome: Incidence of lung cancer (adenocarcinoma analysed separately in the pooled analysis)
lines.magnitude: Pooled analysis of 6 case-control studies (2,159 cases, 2,985 controls; committee's account): habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking OR 0.96 (95% CI 0.66–1.38); among people who did not smoke tobacco OR 1.03 (0.51–2.08); adenocarcinoma only: more than 1 joint a day OR 1.73 (0.75–4.00), more than 10 joint-years OR 1.74 (0.85–3.56), not significant. Swedish conscript cohort (the paper; 1970 to 2009, about 1.9 million person-years; 179 lung cancers among 44,257 in the frequency analysis): more than 50 lifetime uses at conscription against never, HR 2.12 (1.08–4.14) fully adjusted (tobacco in three bands, alcohol, respiratory conditions, socioeconomic status, all at conscription); tobacco-adjusted 2.24 (1.17–4.29); crude 3.72 (1.96–7.06). Fully adjusted, lower bands: once 1.52 (0.77–3.01); 2 to 4 times 0.66 (0.27–1.62); 5 to 10 times 0.68 (0.21–2.16); 11 to 50 times 1.68 (0.77–3.66). Ever against never: crude 1.90 (1.30–2.75), tobacco-adjusted 1.25 (0.85–1.83), fully adjusted 1.25 (0.84–1.87). Tobacco, more than 10 cigarettes a day against none: 5.03 (3.23–7.81). Absolute: 189 lung cancers among 49,321 men by the end of 2009 (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000; editors' calculation); no counts by cannabis group. Committee's grade (its wording): moderate evidence of no statistical association.
lines.reasoning: Observational (case-control studies and one cohort), so the claim starts low. It rests on the National Academies committee's account of the pooled case-control analysis (a narrative review; the pooled analysis was not read, so its figures are second-hand and its risk of bias cannot be appraised, METHODS §6.3) and on the Swedish cohort's own paper, read in full (ROBINS-E high). Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 pass the floor, so the certainty is very low; any two would give the same. The relation is insufficient evidence (METHODS §6.1): neither an effect nor its absence can be shown with precision, because the pooled interval does not exclude a rise of 38% (and, among people who did not smoke tobacco, an odds ratio of 2.08), while the cohort's raised estimate is confined to its heaviest band, with no gradient below it, no association for ever use once tobacco was counted, tobacco smoked by 91% of that band and no estimate possible for men who did not smoke tobacco. The committee's grade, moderate evidence of no statistical association, is its own judgment and concerns statistical significance; the editors do not adopt it as a finding of no effect (METHODS §6.3: no detectable effect needs precision). Not rated as 'causes': every source is observational and none can show cause. The status is mixed (a pooled null and a cohort that points up in one band, not reconciled by the committee; the cohort paper does not resolve it). With the cohort paper read, the claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews; it stays a draft as a section 7 claim held for the senior author.

lines.q: Does smoking cannabis cause lung cancer?
lines.short: Nobody knows yet. Six studies put together found no clear link; a Swedish study found about twice the rate in men who'd used cannabis over 50 times.
lines.but: Of those men, 91 in 100 also smoked tobacco, so the two can't be pulled apart.
how: An expert committee reports that the six studies found no clear link. But a higher risk couldn't be ruled out.
The Swedish study asked young men about cannabis once, at military call-up. Then it followed them for 40 years, until they were about 60.
Men who'd used it over 50 times got lung cancer about twice as often as men who never had, allowing for tobacco smoked then. Less use showed no clear rise.
The Swedish study ended before the age lung cancer is usually found, about 70. The committee notes that cannabis smoke, like tobacco smoke, holds chemicals that cause cancer.

lines.statement: In one laboratory trial of 17 healthy adults who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days (398 days on average), each of whom completed six 8.5-hour sessions at least a week apart, cannabis flower inhaled from a desktop vaporizer, compared with the same flower smoked in a small handheld pipe (10 mg or 25 mg of THC loaded, from 13.4% THC flower, taken over 10 minutes; study conditions only), was associated with higher average peak ratings of drug effect on a 0 to 100 scale at the lower amount (69.5 against 45.7; editors' calculation of the difference, 23.8 points, 95% CI 5.4 to 42.2) but with no flagged difference at the higher amount (77.5 against 66.4), and with a larger rise in heart rate at the lower amount (23.3 against 11.3 beats a minute) but not at the higher. Average peak whole-blood THC was also higher after vaporizing (7.5 against 3.8 ng/mL, and 14.4 against 10.2), but the paper reports no test of that difference and the editors' intervals for it include zero. On attention and psychomotor tasks, three contrasts between the methods were flagged, all showing worse performance after vaporizing; at the higher amount both methods raised ratings of unpleasant effects, anxiety, memory impairment and throat irritation or coughing over placebo, with no flagged difference between them. Three adverse events were reported, all at the higher amount (vomiting once after each method, hallucinations once after vaporizing), too few to compare. Effects outlasted blood THC, which was back to zero within 4 hours while drug-effect ratings were still above baseline at 6 hours. Only some contrasts between the methods were flagged, and none was corrected for the 32 outcomes. The authors say that earlier comparisons (not read here) found similar profiles for the two methods, and suggest that those let people adjust their own dose. This trial gave a fixed amount of one flower to people who rarely use cannabis, with one pipe and one vaporizer, in a laboratory, and followed people only through each session. The authors note that the largest amount given was smaller and weaker than prerolls sold in dispensaries (from a survey they cite, not read here). It did not test joints, bongs, portable vaporizers, oil cartridges, concentrates, tobacco mixed in, self-paced or repeated use, or effects on the lungs, and it did not measure how much THC left each device. Funding as printed: a US federal health agency (SAMHSA), which also provided technical assistance on design, analysis, interpretation and manuscript approval; one author reports consulting fees or honoraria from Zynerba Pharmaceuticals, Insys Therapeutics, Battelle Memorial Institute and Canopy Health Innovations; no industry funding is printed.
lines.population: 17 healthy adults (9 men, 8 women; mean age 27) who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days (mean 398 days since last use, median 365 days)
lines.exposure: Cannabis flower (13.4% THC) vaporized in a desktop vaporizer and inhaled from a balloon, with 10 mg or 25 mg of THC in the material loaded, over 10 minutes (study conditions only)
lines.comparator: The same flower with the same THC loaded, smoked in a small handheld pipe in the same people; each method also had a placebo session (flower under 0.01% THC) as its reference
lines.outcome: Peak ratings of drug effect and other effects, heart rate and blood pressure, whole-blood THC, performance on attention and psychomotor tasks, and adverse events, within 8.5-hour sessions
lines.magnitude: Drug-effect rating (0 to 100), mean (SD) peak: smoked 45.7 (26.4) at 10 mg and 66.4 (28.6) at 25 mg; vaporized 69.5 (26.4) and 77.5 (23.4); placebo 11.2 and 2.1. Vaporized minus smoked, editors' calculation (unpaired, conservative): 23.8 points (95% CI 5.4 to 42.2) at 10 mg; 11.1 (-7.2 to 29.4) at 25 mg. Heart rate rise, beats per minute, mean (SD): smoked 11.3 (10.4) and 19.1 (17.1); vaporized 23.3 (11.8) and 26.8 (16.6); only the 10 mg difference between methods flagged; editors' unpaired differences 12.0 (4.2 to 19.8) and 7.7 (-4.1 to 19.5). Peak whole-blood THC, ng/mL, mean (SD): smoked 3.8 (5.9) and 10.2 (12.4); vaporized 7.5 (5.5) and 14.4 (9.4); no test reported; editors' unpaired differences 3.7 (-0.3 to 7.7) and 4.2 (-3.5 to 11.9). Differences between methods flagged: 4 of 20 rating items at 10 mg and 2 at 25 mg; 3 task contrasts (Divided Attention distance at 10 mg; Digit Symbol Substitution attempted and correct at 25 mg); none corrected across 32 outcomes. Adverse events: 3 reported among 17 people, all in 25 mg sessions. Blood THC back to zero within 4 hours; drug-effect ratings above baseline at 6 hours after both 25 mg conditions.
lines.reasoning: A placebo-controlled within-person laboratory trial with counterbalanced method order and randomized dose order starts high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias -1: RoB 2 'some concerns' in four of six domains (sequence generation not described; method cannot be hidden and the main ratings are self-reported; late registration with 32 uncorrected outcomes). Imprecision -1: 17 people; the lower-amount difference in drug-effect ratings has a wide interval (5.4 to 42.2), the higher-amount difference includes zero, the blood THC difference was not tested, and between-method differences were flagged for only 4 of 20 rating items at the lower amount, 2 at the higher and 3 task contrasts. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is worded for this trial's people and conditions; strict reading: as a claim about vaping against smoking in everyday use it would be indirect and the certainty would be very low. Not downgraded for inconsistency or publication bias on one trial; the earlier comparisons the authors cite, which they say found similar profiles, were not read and would matter if they had been. Worded as an association rather than 'increases' because only some contrasts were flagged, none was corrected for the number of outcomes, and the trial is small.

lines.q: Does vaped cannabis feel different from smoked?
lines.short: It can. In one small lab study, the same cannabis felt stronger vaped than smoked, and raised heart rate more, but only at the lower of two amounts.
lines.but: It's one study of 17 people who rarely use cannabis. Its authors say earlier studies found the two much alike.
how: Each person smoked the same cannabis in a small pipe and vaped it in a desktop vaporizer. Both ways were tested at two amounts, on different days.
At the lower amount, heart rate rose about twice as much after vaping. On the few attention and speed tests where the two ways differed, scores were worse after vaping.
After the higher amount, people still rated an effect when their blood THC was back to zero.
The study didn't test joints, bongs, handheld vapes, oil carts, concentrates, regular use, or the lungs.

lines.statement: In one survey of 2,553 young adults in a Southern California school-based cohort (mean age 19; asked once, between June 2018 and October 2019; 75% took part), people who reported vaping THC or hash oil, or dabs, were more likely to report bronchitic symptoms in the past 12 months (daily cough for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm, or bronchitis) than people who reported never doing so, after adjustment for age, sex, race and ethnicity, financial status, body mass index, nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis: adjusted odds ratios 1.73 (95% CI 1.01 to 2.96) for those whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months earlier, 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56) for 6 months to 30 days earlier, 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47) for 1 or 2 days in the past 30 and 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06) for 3 or more days. Wheeze was raised only in the top band (2.27, 1.17 to 4.37), and shortness of breath was not reliably raised after full adjustment. Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30 was associated with all three symptoms when only age, sex, race, finances and body mass index were adjusted (odds ratios 1.41 to 1.78) and with none after also adjusting for cannabis vaping and smoking (0.85 to 0.96). Overall 17.5% reported bronchitic symptoms (384 of 2,194), 13.0% wheeze and 20.4% shortness of breath; the paper gives no rates by vaping group (editors' rough calculation from its counts: about 12% to 14% of people who never vaped cannabis against about 23% to 31% of those who vaped it on days in the past 30, depending on how people with missing symptom data are counted). The survey was a single snapshot, so which came first is unknown, and symptoms were self-reported with no lung-function test. It did not record the product, device, source or amount vaped, or tobacco mixed into smoked cannabis, and it ran until October 2019, when the national outbreak of vaping-related lung injury (EVALI) was under way, so it cannot show whether the symptoms were linked to the products involved in it. Odds were raised even in people whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months earlier (1.73, against 2.19 to 2.79 for vaping in the past 30 days), which argues for caution about reading the link as an effect of recent vaping and points to residual confounding as a possible explanation. A 2024 systematic review of heart and breathing effects by route (42 sources; nothing pooled; no risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies reported; AMSTAR 2 critically low here; this survey is not among its sources) found no study comparing people who vape cannabis with people who do not use it, and none following people who vape over time. Its vaping evidence, second-hand, compares vaping with smoking: in a laboratory crossover (11 adults who smoked cannabis often and 9 occasionally; dried cannabis in a vaporizer), vaporised cannabis raised exhaled carbon monoxide less than smoked cannabis and breathing rate did not change with either; Canadian medical cannabis patients (a survey of 364) rated vaporizing as less harmful to breathing than smoking; and in a one-month study without a control group, 22 people who used cannabis often and had breathing symptoms switched to a vaporizer, and the 12 who did not develop a respiratory illness reported fewer symptoms and had a higher FVC, with FEV1 not significantly changed. None of these studied THC oil cartridges or dabs, and the survey's authors say longitudinal research is lacking. Funded by the US National Cancer Institute; no conflicts reported.
lines.population: 2,553 young adults (mean age 19.3; 58% women; 47% Hispanic) in a Southern California school-based cohort, surveyed once a year after high-school graduation (outcome data for 2,194 to 2,396)
lines.exposure: Self-reported vaping of THC or hash oil in an electronic device, or dabs, by recency and days of use (lifetime but not past 6 months; past 6 months but not past 30 days; 1 or 2 days in the past 30; 3 or more days in the past 30)
lines.comparator: Young adults in the same survey who reported never vaping cannabis (for the nicotine comparison, never vaping nicotine); the full model also adjusts for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis
lines.outcome: Self-reported bronchitic symptoms (daily cough for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm, or bronchitis) and wheeze in the previous 12 months, and shortness of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill
lines.magnitude: Bronchitic symptoms, cannabis vaping, full-model adjusted odds ratios against never (95% CI): lifetime but not past 6 months 1.73 (1.01 to 2.96); past 6 months but not past 30 days 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56); 1 or 2 days in the past 30 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47); 3 or more days 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06). Wheeze: 1.12 (0.61 to 2.03), 1.47 (0.92 to 2.35), 1.84 (0.88 to 3.86), 2.27 (1.17 to 4.37). Shortness of breath: 0.90 (0.57 to 1.40), 1.25 (0.86 to 1.84), 1.55 (0.81 to 2.96), 1.41 (0.80 to 2.48). Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30, bronchitic symptoms, wheeze, shortness of breath: sociodemographic model 1.78 (1.32 to 2.41), 1.41 (1.01 to 1.96), 1.45 (1.08 to 1.96); full model 0.96 (0.63 to 1.46), 0.85 (0.54 to 1.35), 0.96 (0.64 to 1.42). Absolute: 17.5% (384 of 2,194) bronchitic symptoms, 13.0% (312 of 2,396) wheeze, 20.4% (488 of 2,389) shortness of breath overall; editors' rough calculation for bronchitic symptoms from Table 2 counts: about 12% to 14% in people who never vaped cannabis, about 27% to 31% (1 or 2 days) and 23% to 27% (3 or more days) in those vaping in the past 30 days, depending on how missing symptom data are counted. Editors' note: odds ratios overstate rate ratios when the outcome is this common. 2024 review by route (second-hand; vaping against smoking, not against no use): less exhaled carbon monoxide after vaporised than smoked cannabis from 0.25 to 6 hours and no route effect on breathing rate (laboratory crossover, 11 and 9 adults); lower perceived respiratory harm (survey of 364 medical cannabis patients); fewer symptoms (t(11) = 6.22) and higher FVC (t(11) = 2.90) after a one-month switch in the 12 of 22 who did not develop a respiratory illness, FEV1 not significant (no control group).
lines.reasoning: Observational and cross-sectional, so it starts low. Risk of bias -1: confounding is high, because one time point and coarse adjustment cannot separate cannabis vaping from other exposures (tobacco in joints and blunts, secondhand smoke, asthma) or from reverse causation, and odds were raised as much in people who last vaped cannabis long before the survey as in people who vaped recently. Imprecision -1: several full-model lower bounds sit at 1.01 to 1.04 and the top bands are small. Not upgraded for a large effect (some odds ratios above 2): the most adjusted model still leaves residual confounding that runs away from the null, there is no clear gradient with recency or frequency, and the lower bounds are close to 1. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is worded for self-reported symptoms in this cohort. Rating: very low. Worded as an association, never as an effect of vaping; no longitudinal study of cannabis vaping was read; the 2024 review by route adds only comparisons of vaping with smoking (a laboratory crossover, a perceived-harm survey and an uncontrolled one-month switch with spirometry), second-hand through a review of critically low confidence, which do not change the rating.

lines.q: Is vaping cannabis linked to breathing problems?
lines.short: Yes, in one survey. About 1 in 4 who'd vaped cannabis in the past month reported a lasting cough, phlegm or bronchitis, against 1 in 8 who never had.
lines.but: It's only what people said, once: nobody tested their lungs. So it can't show cause.
how: About 2,500 young adults in Southern California took part. The link held even after allowing for what else they vaped or smoked: nicotine, cigarettes and cannabis.
Even people who hadn't vaped cannabis in over 6 months reported more symptoms. So something else about them may explain part of the link.
The survey didn't ask what people vaped, and it ran into the 2019 outbreak of vaping lung injury (EVALI). So it can't say if those products played a part.
A 2024 review found no study that followed people who vape cannabis over time.

lines.statement: EVALI (e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury) was a surveillance case definition: vaping or dabbing in the previous 90 days, a lung infiltrate on imaging, no other plausible diagnosis, and negative infection testing (confirmed cases) or an infection judged not the sole cause (probable cases). The CDC authors say its high sensitivity likely lowered specificity, so some patients may not have had EVALI. By 14 January 2020 the CDC had been told of 2,668 hospitalized patients (1,401 confirmed, 1,267 probable): median age 24, 66% male; weekly admissions peaked in the week of 15 September 2019 and fell afterwards. Of the 2,022 patients (76%) with information on what they had vaped or dabbed in the previous 3 months, 82% reported a THC-containing product, 57% a nicotine-containing product, 41% both and 14% nicotine only; products were unknown for 24% and were not checked against what was in the devices (in the lung-fluid study, THC or its breakdown products were found in 9 of 11 patients who said they had not used THC products in the 90 days before illness). The CDC authors give three possible reasons for the nicotine-only reports: patients not reporting or not knowing what they vaped, some patients not having EVALI, or accurate reports. Deaths and intensive care are second-hand: CDC figures quoted in the laboratory papers give 52 deaths among about 2,400 reported cases by 12 December 2019 and 47% needing intensive care; the update read gives neither, nor outcomes after discharge. Vitamin E acetate, a form of vitamin E sold online as a diluent or thickener for cannabis oil, was found in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients in 16 states (94%; editors' exact 95% interval 84% to 99%), including all 25 confirmed cases (editors' deduction), and from none of 99 healthy volunteers, none of whom vaped THC (0% to 4%); other additives tested were found in at most one patient. FDA testing, quoted second-hand, found it in 49% of case-associated THC product samples and none of 197 case-associated nicotine products. In 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids from cartridges recovered from 10 New York patients, 23 (64%) held vitamin E acetate (16% to 57% by mass) and 13 held none above 1%; 31 of the 36 held at least one pesticide (editors' count), a pattern the authors judge intermittent and not due to a single pesticide. These findings come from different laboratories, patients and sample types and point the same way, but they do not show cause: the comparison lungs came from people who did not vape THC, so the contrast cannot separate vitamin E acetate from other features of vaping THC products in 2019; no fluid from people who vaped the same products without injury was tested; none of these studies tested whether inhaling it injures the lung (the authors say laboratory studies are needed); the CDC authors state that "evidence is not sufficient to rule out the contribution of other chemicals of concern" in some cases; and a screen of 38 cartridges listed many other chemicals by library match, without counts per cartridge. The cartridge papers call the products illicit or counterfeit; neither describes how this was established. The sources implicate certain vaping products, mostly THC-containing cartridges, and an additive in them. None tested whether THC or cannabis itself injures the lung, or looked at cannabis smoked or eaten or flower vaporized in dry-herb devices; the one screen with medical-grade cartridges (number not stated) found retinol acetate rather than vitamin E acetate in them, and fewer listed contaminants, though some harmful chemicals were identified. So the sources neither show that other forms of cannabis carry this injury nor show that they are free of it. Funding as printed: CDC authors for the surveillance report; National Cancer Institute, FDA Center for Tobacco Products and Ohio State University for the lung-fluid study; none external for the two cartridge studies; no industry funding is printed.
lines.population: People hospitalized with EVALI in the US (2,668 reported to CDC by 14 January 2020); 51 of them with lung fluid tested in 16 states; 10 New York patients whose cartridges were tested (38 samples)
lines.exposure: Vitamin E acetate found in patients' lung fluid and in vaping cartridge fluid (cartridges that held THC or other cannabinoids)
lines.comparator: Lung fluid from 99 healthy volunteers in an unrelated study, none of whom vaped THC; no comparison cartridges within the cartridge studies
lines.magnitude: Surveillance (CDC, 14 January 2020): 2,668 hospitalized (1,401 confirmed, 1,267 probable); median age 24 (13 to 85); 66% male; among 2,022 with product information: any THC 82% (1,650), any nicotine 57% (1,162), both 41% (834), THC only 33% (669), nicotine only 14% (274), neither 2% (44); peak 215 admissions in the week of 15 September 2019. Second-hand: 52 deaths among 2,409 reported cases by 12 December 2019 (about 2%, editors' calculation); 47% needed intensive care in an earlier CDC report. Lung fluid (Blount et al.): vitamin E acetate in 48 of 51 patients (94%; editors' exact 95% CI 83.8% to 98.8%) against 0 of 99 healthy volunteers (0% to 3.7%); 25 of 25 confirmed cases (editors' deduction; 86.3% to 100%) and 23 of 26 probable cases; THC or metabolites 40 of 47 (85%), including 9 of 11 who reported no THC product use; nicotine or metabolites 30 of 47 (64%); coconut oil 1 of 48, limonene 1 of 39, all other priority substances 0 of 12 to 49. Cartridges (Duffy et al.): vitamin E acetate in 23 of 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids (64%; exact 95% CI 46% to 79%, treating fluids as independent) at 16 to 57% by mass, from 10 patients; 13 without it, 12 of which held medium-chain triglyceride oil; 31 of 36 with at least one pesticide (editors' count); update to 12 December 2019 without methods: 101 of 147 THC-containing fluids (69%) from 61 cases; 3 of 6 commercial diluents and thickeners essentially pure vitamin E acetate. Screening (Muthumalage et al.): over 500 chemicals in cartridge liquids; no counts per compound.
lines.reasoning: Observational: a surveillance case series, a case-comparator lung-fluid study and laboratory analyses of cartridges, so it starts low. Risk of bias -1 (all four study cards rated high overall); the rating cannot fall below very low. Not upgraded for a large effect: the 94% against 0% contrast has no adjusted model, and the comparison lungs came from people who did not vape THC and were sampled mostly before 2019, so the contrast probably overstates what separates vitamin E acetate from other features of THC cartridge use in 2019. Not downgraded for inconsistency (the studies agree in direction; the proportions differ for reasons of sample type and source), imprecision (the counts are precise) or indirectness (the claim is worded for the people and products sampled). Strict reading: the presence of vitamin E acetate in nearly all lung fluid tested and in most THC-containing cartridge fluids sampled is consistent across two laboratories, but the rating applies to the association and to the description as worded; that it is the cause or the only cause is a separate claim that none of these studies tests, and is lower still. Status replicated: two independent laboratories (CDC with state laboratories; New York State Department of Health), different patients (New York is not among the 16 states of the lung-fluid study) and different sample types, same direction; a third laboratory (University of Rochester) found it in many but not all cartridge liquids, without counts. The earlier CDC report of 29 patients (whether its patients are among the 51 is not stated) and the New York update of 206 fluids (which presumably includes the 38) are not counted as further replications.

lines.q: What was EVALI, the 2019 lung injury linked to THC vapes?
lines.short: A 2019 US outbreak of serious lung injury in people who vaped; some died. Most said they'd vaped THC. The main suspect is an additive, vitamin E acetate.
lines.but: None of these studies tested whether breathing it in causes the injury. And other chemicals aren't ruled out.
how: By January 2020, 2,668 people had been in US hospitals with it.
Of those who said what they'd vaped, 82 in 100 named a THC product and 14 in 100 only nicotine. Nobody checked their devices.
Vitamin E acetate, sold to cut or thicken cannabis oil, was in the lung fluid of 48 of 51 patients. None of 99 healthy people had it, but they didn't vape THC.
It was also in 23 of 36 cannabis cartridge liquids from New York patients. These studies didn't look at cannabis smoked, eaten or vaped as dried flower.

lines.statement: At one Colorado university hospital's emergency department, 2012 to 2016, clinicians judged 2,567 visits (visits, not people) to be at least partly due to cannabis; 238 (9.3%) were recorded as edible and 2,329 as inhaled (135 of these had no route written down and were counted as inhaled). Compared with inhaled visits, edible visits more often involved intoxication (48.3% against 27.8%; difference 20.5 percentage points, 95% CI 13.9 to 27.1), acute psychiatric symptoms (18.0% against 10.9%; 7.1, 2.1 to 12.1) and cardiovascular symptoms (8.0% against 3.1%; 4.9, 1.4 to 8.4), and less often gastrointestinal symptoms (15.1% against 32.3%; cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4% against 18.0%) or admission to hospital (18.9% against 32.9%); psychiatric symptoms of any kind were similar (26.1% against 24.5%). Severe heart events (heart attack, dangerous heart rhythm) occurred in both groups, with no counts given. Because edibles were under a tenth of the visits, most visits for each of these reasons were inhaled (647 of 762 intoxication visits, 254 of 297 acute psychiatric visits, 73 of 92 cardiovascular visits; editors' arithmetic from the table counts), and the authors write that, given how often inhaled visits occurred and led to admission, education about inhaled cannabis may have the greatest public-health effect. The two groups also differed in who they were (women 51.3% against 33.1%; living outside Colorado 40.8% against 6.6%); a 2016 letter from the same hospital group, cited second-hand in the overview described below and not read, reported that edible-related visits by out-of-state patients rose from 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits between 2013 and 2014, with no significant change for Colorado residents. Against Colorado sales in 2014 to 2016, edibles were 10.7% of this hospital's attributable visits but 0.32% of THC sold by weight, under assumed product contents; the authors call this about 33 times the share expected if the routes were equally likely to lead to a visit, and list its limits (assumed contents, one hospital set against statewide sales, home-grown and illicit supply not counted). A 2016 narrative overview (no stated search or appraisal of studies; its figures are second-hand) quotes another measure, edible units at about 45 percent of Colorado cannabis sales in 2014, without saying how sales were counted, so any such ratio depends on the denominator chosen. No source read here timed effects in patients. The hospital paper and the overview both describe, citing pharmacology work that was not read here, a later and longer effect after eating THC than after inhaling it (the overview: a start within minutes of inhaling against 30 to 90 minutes after eating; the hospital paper: clearance within about 4 hours against about 12). The overview adds that more of the active product 11-OH-THC reaches the blood after eating, which it says may account for stronger, longer-lasting effects; that blood THC after eating is lower than after smoking and tracks intoxication differently from person to person; and that this variation and the delay may lead people to take more than intended before the effect starts, which its abstract says often results in profoundly adverse effects (no count given). The hospital paper cites a consumer survey and an analysis of Twitter posts (neither read) in which people report longer-lasting effects with edibles than with smoking or vaping, and more intense effects and unpleasant psychiatric symptoms. The overview relays anecdotal reports from patients, including patients who took cannabis daily, of eating a whole product after feeling no effect from a first serving, and describes one death in Colorado in 2014 (a 19-year-old man; the autopsy named cannabis intoxication a chief contributing factor) after he ate the whole cookie within two hours of a first serving, having not felt intoxicated within an hour (a public-health case report, as cited). The hospital paper cites three deaths linked to edibles from news reports; none of its 2,567 visits ended in death. No source read here counts how often people eat more after a slow start. What these sources cannot show: how many people took each form (shares of visits are not the chance that a form leads to a visit); who took which form (no adjustment); how much was eaten (a dose was charted for 130 of the 2,567 visits, 80 of them edible; the authors could not verify doses, say eaten doses may have been larger than inhaled ones, and were surprised that the charted edible doses were low); what the products contained (not tested in the hospital study; a separate laboratory test of other products found most of them more than 10% away from their labels; see the claim on edible labels); and what happened to people who took cannabis without harm or did not attend hospital (the authors note that most people who take cannabis may have no adverse effect). Route came from chart notes and patients' own accounts, and the authors say counting undocumented routes as inhaled could bias toward more illness in the inhaled group. Inhaled visits were not split by product (flower, vaped oil, concentrates) or checked for tobacco mixed in, and no comparison was made with people who do not use cannabis. The overview states that edible products account for most health-care visits for cannabis intoxication, citing a 2015 viewpoint not read here; the hospital count has edibles at 115 of 762 intoxication visits (15.1%). The overview also infers that eating cannabis does not seem to affect lung function or cancer risk, citing no study of people who eat cannabis. A 2024 systematic review of heart and breathing effects by route (42 sources; nothing pooled or appraised; AMSTAR 2 critically low here; this hospital study is not among its sources) also found no study of the lungs of adults who eat cannabis. Its oral-route evidence, second-hand, is a laboratory crossover in which heart rate rose about as much after eating cannabis as after smoking or vaporising it (about 10 to 13 beats a minute above placebo) and breathing rate did not change with route; a survey in which Canadian medical cannabis patients rated eating as less harmful to breathing than smoking; and records of children who ate cannabis products (calls to US poison centres and two hospital chart reviews), in which a fast heart rate was common, some children needed help with breathing, and severe heart and breathing effects were seen at higher doses for their body weight. Its abstract nonetheless says edibles were associated with minimal respiratory effects. Follow-up was the visit itself: the hospital data do not follow anyone afterwards, and the overview has no data of its own.   Funding as printed: the hospital paper, the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (competitive grant; the paper says the funder had no part in design, analysis, interpretation or dissemination), with the first author's NIH support and membership of the Colorado Retail Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee; the overview, RTI International internal funds and a US National Institute on Drug Abuse grant, with no conflict statement printed; No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding is printed for the hospital paper or the overview.
lines.population: 2,567 emergency visits (median age 30; 65.2% male; 9.8% from outside Colorado) to one Colorado university hospital, 2012 to 2016, that clinicians judged at least partly due to cannabis: 238 recorded as edible and 2,329 as inhaled. Visits, not people (for example, 301 people accounted for 440 of the visits for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome). Timing and case-report material comes from a 2016 narrative overview citing laboratory studies and case reports (not read).
lines.exposure: Cannabis recorded in the chart as eaten or drunk (edible; 238 visits), from the nursing questionnaire and providers' notes, self-reported and unverified; a dose was charted for 80 of the 238 (study measure only); product contents not tested in the hospital study.
lines.comparator: Visits recorded as inhaled (2,194 documented as smoked or otherwise inhaled, plus 135 with no route written down, counted as inhaled) at the same hospital in the same years. No comparison group of people who took each form and did not attend hospital, and no comparison with people who do not use cannabis; for the sales comparison, flower and edible units sold in Colorado in 2014 to 2016 under assumed THC contents.
lines.outcome: Reasons for the visit coded from the chart (intoxication; acute, acute-on-chronic and chronic psychiatric symptoms; gastrointestinal symptoms including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; cardiovascular symptoms), admission and length of stay; the later and longer effect after eating as described from cited pharmacology and case reports, not measured in patients.
lines.magnitude: Hospital chart review (Monte 2019), share of each group's visits, edible-attributed (n = 238) against inhaled-attributed (n = 2,329), % (difference in percentage points, 95% CI): intoxication 48.3 vs 27.8 (20.5; 13.9 to 27.1); acute psychiatric symptoms 18.0 vs 10.9 (7.1; 2.1 to 12.1); cardiovascular symptoms 8.0 vs 3.1 (4.9; 1.4 to 8.4); any psychiatric symptom 26.1 vs 24.5 (1.6; -4.2 to 7.4); gastrointestinal symptoms 15.1 vs 32.3 (-17.2; -22.1 to -12.2), of which cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4 vs 18.0 (-9.6; -13.5 to -5.7); admitted 18.9 vs 32.9; women 51.3 vs 33.1; living outside Colorado 40.8 vs 6.6 (each P < 0.001); median length of stay 2 hours (range 1 to 54) vs 3 hours (0 to 121). Severe heart events (myocardial infarction, ventricular dysrhythmia) in both groups, no counts. Edible-attributed visits as a share of all visits for each reason, editors' arithmetic from Table 2 counts: intoxication 115 of 762 (15.1%), acute psychiatric 43 of 297 (14.5%), cardiovascular 19 of 92 (20.7%); edible 238 of 2,567 visits (9.3%). Route recorded in 2,432 of 2,567 visits (94.7%); dose charted in 130 (5.1%), 80 of them edible, 19 of those at 50 mg of THC or more (as charted, unverified; study measure only). Eight symptom groups compared, no correction for multiple comparisons. Colorado sales 2014 to 2016: 219 edible and 1,819 inhaled attributable visits (edible 10.7%); edible 0.32% of THC sold by weight (flower 327,990 kg at an assumed 20% THC; 21.2 million edible units at an assumed 10 mg each); flower-to-edible THC ratio 309 (range 279 to 325); visit share about 33 times the share expected if both routes were equally likely to lead to a visit (authors). Overview (Barrus 2016, narrative, second-hand figures): Colorado 2014 edible units 1.96 million medicinal and 2.85 million retail, said to be about 45 percent of total cannabis sales (measure not stated); timing as cited, inhaled start within minutes and effects tapering within 2 to 3 hours, eaten start 30 to 90 minutes and peak 2 to 4 hours after eating (hospital paper, from the same pharmacology review: clearance about 4 hours after inhaling, about 12 hours after eating); oral bioavailability 6 to 10 percent of the amount in the product (as cited); 83 percent of tested medicinal edibles more than 10 percent from their labelled THC (second-hand; the paper itself, now read, gives 62 of 75, 82.7%, editors' arithmetic); out-of-state patients' edible-related visits 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits, 2013 to 2014 (second-hand, not read).
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). The route comparison rests on one chart review at one hospital and a narrative overview with no data of its own. Risk of bias -1: ROBINS-E overall high for the chart review (no adjustment; route self-reported and presumed inhaled when undocumented; every person in the data attended an emergency department); the overview has no stated search or appraisal and its figures are second-hand. Indirectness -1: one hospital in an area of high availability; edible against inhaled only; timing and the 11-OH-THC explanation come from pharmacology work that was not read and were not measured in patients; the sales ratio rests on assumed contents. Imprecision -1: 238 edible visits, wide intervals for two of the three findings that favour more events with edibles, no correction across eight symptom groups, a dose charted for 5.1% of visits. These downgrades together pass the floor, so the certainty is very low. Not downgraded for inconsistency or publication bias: one data set per question; the overview's statement that edibles account for most intoxication visits conflicts with the hospital count (15.1%) but rests on a viewpoint that was not read, so it is shown as a contradicting anchor and flagged. Worded as 'describes' rather than 'increases' or 'is associated with' because the data are shares of visits, not risks, with no count of people taking each form, and the claim combines counts, the authors' interpretation and second-hand pharmacology. The Discussion's causal wording and the 33-fold ratio are the authors' own reading and are reported as such, not adopted.

lines.q: What goes wrong with cannabis edibles, compared with smoking or vaping?
lines.short: Different things. In one US ER, visits after edibles were more often for being too high, or for sudden mental-health or heart symptoms. After smoking or vaping: vomiting.
lines.but: These are shares of ER visits, not risks. Nobody counted how many people used each form.
how: Being too high came up in 48 in 100 visits after edibles, against 28 in 100 after smoking or vaping.
Edibles were only about 1 in 11 of the ER's cannabis visits. So most visits for each problem still followed smoking or vaping.
A dose was written down in about 1 in 20 visits, and couldn't be checked. The authors say eaten doses may have been bigger than inhaled ones.
Papers citing lab work say eating acts later and lasts longer than inhaling. A review says the delay may lead people to take more than they meant.

lines.statement: A laboratory test of products, read with its July 2015 correction (whose wording is followed where the saved letter differs), measured 75 labelled edible products of 47 brands (baked goods, drinks, candy or chocolate) bought in August to October 2014 at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle, in markets the authors call unregulated. Against the THC printed on the package, 13 (17%) were within 10%, 17 (23%) held more than the label said (on average 28% more, at most 55% more) and 45 (60%) held less (on average about half the labelled amount: 47% less in the table's overall row, about 53% less from its city rows, editors' arithmetic; at most 99% less, some with almost none). Products holding more than their label were commonest in Los Angeles (9 of 20) and products holding less in Seattle (18 of 23, where 1 product was within 10%); San Francisco had 8 of 32 within 10% (χ² = 12.94, P = .01). Only 13 products printed a CBD content, and none held it within 10% (4 more, 9 less; editors' arithmetic), although 44 of the 75 contained some CBD. Whole packages were mixed before testing, so the test cannot say how evenly THC was spread between pieces or servings (two samples of the same mixed package differed by more than 10% in 37 products, which were then analysed whole), and it measured no effects in people: the authors' statements that products with less THC may not give the intended medical benefit and that products with more put patients at risk of adverse effects are their inference. The sample was not random and may not generalize, as the authors say, and the cost of the testing was covered by Werc Shop Laboratories, with which four of the six authors are affiliated (see funding). Funding as printed: the label test, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, except the cost of the laboratory testing, which Werc Shop Laboratories covered (four of the six authors are affiliated with Werc Shop Laboratory; the paper says neither funder had any role in the design, conduct, analysis or reporting, while its list of contributions credits two of those four with the concept, design and supervision of the study; one author reported personal fees and nonfinancial support from Tilray (Division of Privateer Holdings) and travel reimbursement from Americans for Safe Access; the paper does not say what these organisations do).
lines.population: 75 labelled edible products (products, not people) bought at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle, August to October 2014.
lines.exposure: the THC and CBD measured in each whole package by laboratory chromatography.
lines.comparator: the THC or CBD content printed on the package, within 10% counted as accurate.
lines.outcome: measured content within 10% of the label, more than 10% above it, or more than 10% below it.
lines.magnitude: Label test (Vandrey 2015, as corrected in JAMA 2015;314(2):188; products, not people): 75 labelled edibles of 47 brands (22 baked goods, 13 beverages, 40 candy or chocolate; editors' sums), nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in three cities, August to October 2014; measured THC against the label: within 10%, 13 (17%; Wilson 95% CI 10.4 to 27.4, editors' calculation); more than 10% above, 17 (23%; 14.7 to 33.3); more than 10% below, 45 (60%; 48.7 to 70.3); outside 10%, 62 (82.7%; 72.6 to 89.6). Mean deviation (SD): within, -3% (4); above, +28% (13), largest +55%; below, -47% (29) in the overall row, against -52.5% from the city rows (-44%, -55% and -61% for 20, 7 and 18 products; editors' arithmetic), largest -99%. By city, within / above / below: San Francisco 8 / 4 / 20 of 32; Los Angeles 4 / 9 / 7 of 20; Seattle 1 / 4 / 18 of 23 (χ² = 12.94, P = .01; degrees of freedom not printed; 3 of 9 expected counts below 5, editors' calculation). By type, within / above / below: baked goods 2 / 7 / 13; beverages 3 / 2 / 8; candy or chocolate 8 / 8 / 24. CBD detected in 44 (59%); printed on 13, of which 4 above and 9 below the label (none within 10%, editors' arithmetic); median THC:CBD 36:1. Measured THC per package (measured product content): median 54 mg, range under 1 to 1,236 mg; labelled 2 to 1,000 mg. Duplicate samples differed by more than 10% in 37 of 75.
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). One laboratory test of 75 products: indirectness -1 (three US cities, medical dispensaries, 2014, unregulated markets) and imprecision -1 (75 products, wide interval), so the certainty is very low. Worded as 'describes' because it measures product content, not effects in people; the authors' statements about benefit and risk are their inference.

lines.q: Do cannabis edible labels show how much THC is inside?
lines.short: Mostly not, in a 2014 US test. Only 17 in 100 cannabis edibles matched their THC label; 60 in 100 held less and 23 in 100 more.
lines.but: It's one test of 75 edibles, not picked at random, from markets its authors call unregulated. Products and rules may have changed since.
how: They came from medical-cannabis shops in three US cities. A lab measured each package's THC; within a tenth of the label counted as a match.
Those with less THC than labelled held about half the labelled amount on average, and some almost none. Those with more held about 28% more on average.
Each package was mixed before testing, so the test can't say how evenly THC was spread between pieces. No effects on people were measured.
Werc Shop Laboratories, linked to four of the six authors, paid for the tests.

lines.statement: In one Colorado field study of 121 adults who already used cannabis at least four times a month (55 using flower, 66 using concentrates; each person chose the form, and a labelled strength was assigned at random within each form), blood THC measured about 13 minutes after they used their own product in their own way at home was higher in the concentrate group than in the flower group (mean 0.32 against 0.14 µg/mL), and so was the active by-product 11-OH-THC, at every time point including before use. Even so, self-rated intoxication (form effect P = .11) and the marijuana effects scale (P = .18) did not differ by form, tension and vigor ratings were lower in the concentrate group, and inhibitory control scores were higher in the flower group at every time, including before use. Delayed verbal recall worsened after use in both groups (form effect P = .65), and eyes-closed balance worsened and was back at its pre-use level by one hour in both (form effect P = .85); the main text reports no effects of labelled strength within a form at its set threshold (P < .01), with the strength tests in a supplement that was not read. The authors offer three untested explanations for similar intoxication despite higher blood THC (greater tolerance in the concentrate group, receptor saturation, individual differences) and read the lack of a blood-level difference by strength within a form as suggesting that people adjust how much they take. The groups were not alike before the session: the concentrate group had used concentrates on 16.5 of the past 30 days against 3.5, had begun regular use at 17.7 years against 20.0 and had about twice the baseline THC metabolite, and it used about half as much product by weight at the session. There was no placebo or no-use session, so changes after use cannot be told apart from repeating the tests; follow-up was one hour; form was not randomised, so earlier differences between the groups may account for some findings; 12 of the 133 people assessed were left out because blood THC after use was very low (9 of 64 on flower, 3 of 69 on concentrates; editors' arithmetic from the group sizes); and people had to have used the strongest product they could be assigned before without a bad reaction and to use no other drugs or daily tobacco, so the findings do not reach people who use cannabis rarely, are new to it, or do not use it. Tobacco mixed into joints was not recorded and cannabinoids other than THC were not reported. The authors' Conclusions voice concern about long-term effects, which were not measured, and the Abstract and Results print the spread of blood THC as standard errors although the Discussion gives standard deviations. A scoping review done for the State of Colorado searched seven databases to mid-2022 and mapped 452 human studies that report a THC concentration or a high-concentration product (225 observational studies, 142 randomised trials, 51 case reports and 34 case series; earliest 1971, 60% published 2017 to 2022). Only 54 (12%) examined concentrates and a health outcome directly and 189 (42%) examined THC concentration directly; 63% studied generic cannabis types, and products typically high in concentration (oils, concentrates, hash, extracts, resins) were examined in about 2% to 10% of studies. The median strength studied was 12% THC where given as a percentage (15 mg where given in milligrams), well below the Colorado market strengths the authors cite from other sources for 2020 (flower averaging 19%, concentrates 68%), which they think likely reflects the restriction of research cannabis to a federal supply without concentrates. Only 47% of studies had a control group and 41% reported effect estimates, and most did not capture the elements of use needed to estimate exposure. The review extracted no study results and did not assess bias, so it shows what has been studied and not what was found; its Conclusions say the literature has serious limits in generalisability to the current market and that high-quality evidence bearing on whether to regulate THC concentration is scarce. Searches were English-only, designed to be sensitive rather than specific, and screened with AI assistance, so studies may be missing; the evidence map and the appendix were not read. Of the 452 studies, 25 (6%) were funded by the cannabis industry and 58 (13%) had an author with a disclosed industry tie, while 24% reported no funding source and 32% no conflict statement. A systematic review of observational studies searched to January 2021 (Petrilli et al., 2022; 20 articles from 16 studies by the editors' count, none rated good quality, no meta-analysis because every study relied on what people said they used and definitions of strength differed) found stronger cannabis (skunk-type, or types of 10% THC or more) associated with psychosis in two case-control studies and one cohort, all rated fair: against never-use, first-episode psychosis was more likely with skunk-type use in a UK study (adjusted odds ratio 2.91, 95% CI 1.52 to 3.60) and with types of 10% THC or more across six countries (1.6, 1.2 to 2.2; 4.8 with daily use), but not with hash-type or lower-strength use (0.83; 1.1), and relapse after a first episode was more likely with continued daily use of stronger cannabis (3.28, 1.22 to 9.18, against former use); none of these three studies looked at concentrates as a separate form. Findings for anxiety and depression varied. The studies of concentrates themselves were all cross-sectional and rated poor: in a 20-country online survey of 181,870 people, those who used butane hash oil more often reported a past diagnosis of anxiety (odds ratio 1.80, 1.60 to 2.01) or depression (1.34, 1.21 to 1.48) than those who used lower-strength herbal cannabis, but not of psychosis (1.11, 0.85 to 1.46); a US sample of 156 found no clear association of concentrate use with psychosis, anxiety or depression symptoms, and another of 191 no difference in anxiety or depression between people who frequently used concentrates and people who frequently used herbal cannabis; in a within-person survey of 574 people, mostly using infrequently, psychosis-like experiences were slightly less frequent with concentrates than with herbal cannabis (Cohen's d 0.12); and among 71 Japanese patients, liquid or resin forms went with less residual or late-onset psychosis than dry herbal cannabis (odds ratio 0.21, 0.06 to 0.74). The review's findings on strength and cannabis use disorder are set out in a separate claim. Its authors argue that people taking less of stronger products would weaken rather than inflate these associations, and that people with poorer mental health may choose stronger products. No study read here follows people who use concentrates beyond one hour, compares them with people who do not use cannabis, or reports lung or other long-term physical outcomes for concentrates. Funding as printed: the field study, the US National Institutes of Health and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, with the paper stating that the funders had no role in the study; participants bought their products at one local dispensary that set aside allotments for the study, with no payment declared; the review, the State of Colorado under House Bill 21-1317 (funder not involved), with authors' interests as printed (a paid consultancy for Health Canada on conflict of interest, a paid UpToDate chapter, research funding from the Institute of Cannabis Research and a seat on the state health department's marijuana advisory committee); the systematic review, an Economic and Social Research Council doctoral studentship, Cancer Research UK fellowship and project awards and a Wellcome Trust grant (funder without a role), with one author reporting previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and a scientific consulting company doing unrelated work, and its senior author an author of several of the studies it reviews, including the butane hash oil survey. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed for any of the three papers.
lines.population: 121 adults in Colorado (mean age about 28; 42% to 48% women) who used cannabis at least four times a month, had used the strongest product they could be assigned before without a bad reaction, and used no other non-prescription drugs or daily tobacco (Bidwell 2020); and 452 human studies that report a THC concentration or a high-concentration product, 1971 to 2022 (Bero 2023, scoping review); and 16 observational studies in 20 articles of people who use cannabis, people with psychosis and population controls, and people using medical cannabis, in Europe, the Americas and Japan and in online surveys across 20 and 175 countries (Petrilli 2022, systematic review).
lines.exposure: Concentrates (laboratory-tested, labelled 70% or 90% THC, assigned at random within the form; the form itself self-chosen), used in the person's usual way at home (glass rig or tube 92%, hash pen 8%) in one session after 5 days of free use (study conditions only); in the review, studies of concentrates or other high-concentration products and of THC concentration; in the systematic review, self-reported use of concentrates (butane hash oil, concentrates, or liquid or resin forms) or of stronger herbal cannabis (skunk-type, or types of 10% THC or more), as each study defined them.
lines.comparator: Flower (labelled 16% or 24% THC; pipe 51%, bong 31%, vaporizer 11%, joint 7%) in a separate group of regular consumers who chose flower; no placebo or no-use session, and no people who do not use cannabis. In the review, no comparison of outcomes (an inventory of studies). In the systematic review, lower-strength herbal cannabis, hash-type cannabis or never-use, as each study defined them; the concentrate studies compared people who use cannabis in different forms, never with people who do not use cannabis.
lines.outcome: Blood THC and 11-OH-THC, self-rated intoxication and marijuana-effects scale, mood (tension, vigor), delayed verbal recall, inhibitory control and working memory, and balance, before use, about 13 minutes after use and 1 hour after use. In the review, counts of studies by exposure, outcome, design and reporting. In the systematic review, psychosis (first episode, relapse, symptoms, self-reported diagnosis), psychosis-like experiences, and anxiety and depression (diagnosis or symptoms); its cannabis use disorder findings are in a separate claim.
lines.magnitude: Field study (Bidwell 2020), concentrate group (n = 66) against flower group (n = 55), means before use, about 13 minutes after use (mean 13.3, range 3 to 47) and 1 hour after use. Blood THC, µg/mL: concentrate 0.01, 0.32, 0.03; flower 0.004, 0.14, 0.02; form effect F(1,228) = 11.00, P < .01. 11-OH-THC, µg/mL: concentrate 0.004, 0.011, 0.008; flower 0.001, 0.005, 0.004; form effect P < .001. Self-rated intoxication (scale range inconsistently described in the paper): concentrate 0.14, 2.35, 1.63; flower 0.08, 2.40, 1.93; form effect P = .11. Marijuana effects scale: form effect P = .18. Tension and vigor lower in the concentrate group (P < .01 and P < .001). Delayed verbal recall errors: concentrate 0.90, 1.50, 2.33; flower 0.65, 2.21, 1.88; change after use P < .001; form effect P = .65; form by quadratic time P = .02 (above the set threshold). Eyes-closed sway: concentrate 0.64, 0.69, 0.64; flower 0.63, 0.73, 0.63; quadratic time P < .001; form effect P = .85. Inhibitory control higher in the flower group at every time (P < .001). Thirteen outcomes tested at a fixed threshold of P < .01; no placebo. Baseline, concentrate against flower group: concentrate use on 16.5 vs 3.5 of the past 30 days; regular use begun at 17.7 vs 20.0 years; THC-COOH 0.087 vs 0.044 µg/mL; product used at the session 0.11 g vs 0.22 g (study measure only). Labelled strengths assigned at random within form: flower 16% or 24%, concentrate 70% or 90% THC; groups of 26 to 33 people. 133 assessed (64 flower, 69 concentrate); 12 left out for post-use blood THC below 0.02 µg/mL (9 flower, 3 concentrate). Scoping review (Bero 2023): 49,729 unique records, 5,828 full texts, 452 studies (225 observational, 142 randomised trials, 51 case reports, 34 case series); 54 (12%) concentrates and an outcome directly, 189 (42%) THC concentration and an outcome directly, 114 (25%) and 62 (14%) indirectly; control group in 212 (47%); effect estimates in 184 (41%); generic cannabis types in 284 (63%); products typically high in concentration in about 2% to 10%; THC given as a percentage in 172 studies, median 12% (mean 17.4%, range 0% to 100%, interquartile range 3.6% to 24%), and in milligrams in 113, median 15 mg (mean 37.4, range 0.3 to 500, interquartile range 7.5 to 26); market strengths cited by the authors from other sources for Colorado: flower averaging 14% (2014) to 19% (2020), concentrates 46% to 68%. Funding of the included studies: 25 (6%) cannabis industry, 58 (13%) author with an industry tie, 109 (24%) no funding source reported, 143 (32%) no conflict statement. Outcome domains most studied: mental health 40%, neurologic 30%, pain 29%, cardiometabolic 24%, gastrointestinal 22%, psychosocial 22%, sleep 21%. Systematic review (Petrilli 2022; 16 studies in 20 articles, none rated good): psychosis, adjusted odds ratios against never-use, skunk-type 2.91 (95% CI 1.52 to 3.60) and hash-type 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77) in the UK GAP study; types of 10% THC or more 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2) and under 10% 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5) in the six-country EU-GEI study, daily use 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6); relapse with continued daily use of stronger cannabis 3.28 (1.22 to 9.18) against former use (58% against 24% relapsed). Concentrate studies (cross-sectional, rated poor): butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal cannabis in a 20-country survey of 181,870, self-reported diagnosis of anxiety 1.80 (1.60 to 2.01), depression 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48), psychosis 1.11 (0.85 to 1.46); concentrate use in 156 US adults, psychosis symptoms r 0.11 (-0.20 to 0.40), anxiety 0.21 (-0.10 to 0.49), depression 0.17 (-0.15 to 0.45); frequent concentrate against frequent herbal use in 191 US adults, anxiety means 1.1 and 0.66, depression 0.72 and 0.76, not significantly different; psychosis-like experiences in 574 people, means 1.1 with concentrates and 1.2 with herbal cannabis (0 to 10 scale; Cohen's d 0.12); 71 Japanese patients, liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis, residual or late-onset psychotic disorder 0.212 (0.061 to 0.735). Anxiety and depression with higher- against lower-potency herbal cannabis: generalised anxiety disorder 1.92 (1.11 to 3.32) in a UK sample of 1,087; 1.05 (0.98 to 1.12) for anxiety and 1.18 (1.11 to 1.25) for depression in the 20-country survey; major depression 1.28 (0.68 to 2.32) in the UK sample.
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). The field study randomised labelled strength within each form but not the form, so the concentrate-against-flower comparison that this claim reports is observational. Risk of bias -1: ROBINS-E overall high (self-chosen form with baseline differences in concentrate use, years of regular use and THC metabolite; selected volunteers; no placebo or no-use session; exclusion of 12 people by an outcome; thirteen outcomes at a fixed threshold). The scoping review adds counts of what has been studied and no results, and is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (provisional: the appendix was not read) chiefly because it does not appraise the studies it maps. Indirectness -1: regular consumers, one dispensary, one session, blood at about 13 minutes and 1 hour, impairment inferred without a placebo. Imprecision -1: 121 people, 26 to 33 per strength group, no confidence intervals, null form effects from a study not built to show equivalence, results at P = .02 and P = .05 unresolved. These downgrades together pass the floor, so the certainty is very low. Not downgraded for inconsistency or publication bias: one field study. Worded as 'is associated with' because each person chose the form and the groups differed at baseline; the statement of what the scoping review found is a statement about the literature, not about health effects. The systematic review added in version 0.3.0 (Petrilli 2022; AMSTAR 2 low confidence, provisional) qualifies the claim without changing its rating: the psychosis associations it reports for stronger cannabis come from case-control and cohort studies that did not look at concentrates as a separate form, and its studies of concentrates and mental health are cross-sectional, rated poor and inconsistent with one another.

lines.q: Are cannabis concentrates like wax and shatter riskier than flower?
lines.short: Nobody knows yet. In one study, people using cannabis concentrates had over twice the blood THC of people using flower. Yet they didn't rate themselves higher.
lines.but: It's one study of 121 people who use cannabis often, followed for just an hour.
how: Memory and balance got worse after use in both groups, with no clear gap between them.
The concentrate group already used concentrates far more often. More tolerance might explain why they didn't feel higher, the authors suggest, but that wasn't tested.
A review for Colorado found only 54 of 452 studies looked directly at concentrates and health. The typical strength studied was well below what's sold now.
Another review linked stronger plant cannabis, like skunk, to psychosis. Its studies of concentrates and mental health were rated poor. They asked people once, and disagreed.

lines.statement: In people who use cannabis, using cannabis of higher strength, as each study defined it (stronger herbal types such as skunk or sinsemilla, types of 10% THC or more, hash in one survey, liquid or resin forms in one clinical sample, or concentrates), compared with lower-strength cannabis, is associated with more signs of cannabis use disorder in four of the six studies found by a systematic review searched to January 2021 (Petrilli et al., 2022), all of them cross-sectional, one rated fair and five poor. In a UK annual drug survey of 2,514 people, each extra day a month of using skunk went with a Severity of Dependence Scale score 0.25 points higher (scale 0 to 15, 3 or more taken to indicate dependence; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.36), with no association for grass or resin (adjusted for age and gender); in a survey of 55,240 people from 175 countries, the groups using sinsemilla or hashish alongside herbal cannabis scored 0.16 and 0.26 points higher than the group using herbal cannabis only (adjusted for age, gender, amount and frequency of use and tobacco added); in a UK sample of 1,087 people aged about 24, people who used stronger cannabis were more likely to report recent cannabis problems on a screening test (adjusted odds ratio 4.08, 95% CI 1.41 to 11.81, adjusted for frequency of use, age at first use, sex and childhood socio-economic position); and among 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders, people who used liquid or resin forms more often had a dependence syndrome than people who used dry herbal cannabis (odds ratio 6.85, 95% CI 1.87 to 25.15 in the table, 1.19 to 25.15 in the text; no adjustment listed). The two studies that compared concentrates with herbal cannabis found no clear difference: in 156 US adults, neither concentrate nor stronger herbal use was associated with use-disorder symptoms (the interval printed for concentrates does not contain its own estimate), and in 191 US adults, people who frequently used concentrates did not report significantly more symptoms than people who frequently used herbal cannabis (means 2.1 and 1.3, with few symptoms overall). Every study relied on what people said they used; none measured THC in their cannabis or how much they took in, only one adjusted for the amount used, and no study followed people over time or compared them with people who do not use cannabis. The review's Discussion says higher-strength use was "consistently associated with an increased risk of CUD", which is stronger than these results. Its senior author is an author of three of the four studies that found an association (the two surveys and the UK sample, which another review author led); the Japanese study and the two studies that found no clear difference are by other groups. A later narrative review (Inman & Cservenka, online 2024; 27 articles found through PubMed and citation searches, not appraised) says that studies have consistently linked concentrate use with a higher cannabis use disorder risk than other forms, citing mainly the survey of 191 people as showing more symptoms, together with US college and web surveys that compare people by how often they use concentrates; it does not cite the systematic review. It finds little information on cannabis use disorder with edibles and argues only by analogy with slower-acting forms of other drugs, and concludes that how often people use cannabis remains the most reliable predictor across all forms and that a causal role of strength is not established. As a base rate, a meta-analysis of 21 general-population studies from high-income countries (Leung et al., 2020; studies published 2009 to 2020, over half from the US, mostly DSM-IV) puts the share of people who had used cannabis who met criteria for cannabis use disorder at 22 in 100 (95% CI 18 to 26) and for dependence at 13 in 100 (10 to 15), pooling lifetime, past-year and past-month measures, with single studies ranging from 4.5 in 100 (US adults aged 50 or more) to 41 in 100 (21-year-olds in one Australian cohort); dependence was 33 in 100 (22 to 44) in two cohorts of young people who used weekly or daily, against 18 in 100 (12 to 24) in cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use. That review found no population study that estimated the risk by the strength of the cannabis used, and it did not appraise the studies it pooled. Funding as printed: the systematic review, an Economic and Social Research Council doctoral studentship, Cancer Research UK fellowship and project awards and a Wellcome Trust grant (funder without a role), with one author reporting previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and a consulting company doing unrelated work; the narrative review, no funding and no conflicts; the meta-analysis, University of Queensland and NHMRC fellowships and Australian Government Drug and Alcohol Program funding of the authors' centre, with no conflicts. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
lines.population: People who use cannabis: respondents to drug surveys (a UK annual survey, n = 2,514; a survey across 175 countries, n = 55,240), a UK sample of 1,087 people aged about 24, US convenience samples of 156 and 191 adults, and 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders (Petrilli 2022, six cross-sectional studies); US surveys of college students, high-school students, adults and web samples (Inman 2026, narrative review); and, for the base rate, people who had ever, recently or regularly used cannabis in 21 general-population studies from the US, Australia, New Zealand, Germany, the Netherlands, Ireland and France (Leung 2020).
lines.exposure: Self-reported use of higher-strength cannabis as each study defined it: skunk, sinsemilla or other stronger herbal types; types typically of 10% THC or more; hash classed with stronger types in one survey; liquid or resin forms in one clinical sample; concentrates (including butane hash oil) in the two US samples and the narrative review, which also compares flower and edibles as forms. Strength bands are study definitions only. For the base rate, any cannabis use (ever, past year or month, or weekly or daily).
lines.comparator: Lower-strength cannabis as each study defined it (grass, resin or herbal types; types typically under 10% THC; dry herbal cannabis); in the two concentrate studies, people who use herbal cannabis (frequently, in one). No study compared with people who do not use cannabis. For the base rate, none (a share of people who had used cannabis).
lines.outcome: Signs of cannabis use disorder: Severity of Dependence Scale scores (0 to 15; 3 or more taken to indicate dependence), recent problems on the Cannabis Abuse Screening Test, a MINI cannabis screening test, a self-report symptom questionnaire, or ICD-10 dependence syndrome by clinical interview; for the base rate, DSM-III-R, DSM-IV (abuse or dependence) or DSM-5 cannabis use disorder from structured interviews.
lines.magnitude: Systematic review (Petrilli 2022), six cross-sectional studies, higher against lower strength: Severity of Dependence Scale b 0.254 (95% CI 0.161 to 0.357) per extra day a month of skunk use, grass 0.020 (-0.029 to 0.070), resin 0.025 (-0.019 to 0.067) (UK survey, 2,514; poor); b 0.155 (0.100 to 0.209) for sinsemilla with herbal and 0.262 (0.188 to 0.337) for hashish with herbal against herbal only (175-country survey, 55,240; poor); recent problems, adjusted odds ratio 4.08 (1.41 to 11.81) (UK sample, 1,087; fair); dependence syndrome, odds ratio 6.85 (1.87 to 25.15 in Table 2; 1.19 to 25.15 in the text) for liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis (71 Japanese patients; poor); no association in 156 US adults (stronger herbal r 0.09, -0.12 to 0.30; concentrates -0.05, interval printed as -0.35 to -0.26; poor); no significant difference between frequent concentrate and frequent herbal use in 191 US adults (mean symptoms 2.1 against 1.3; poor). Narrative review (Inman 2026): no effect sizes.
