Base rate (Leung 2020; 21 studies, 153 data points, high-income countries): cannabis use disorder 22 in 100 (18 to 26), abuse 13 in 100 (8 to 18), dependence 13 in 100 (10 to 15) among people who had used cannabis; use disorder by design and recall period, 17 in 100 (12 to 23) to 28 in 100 (10 to 48); dependence with weekly or daily use 33 in 100 (22 to 44) in two cohorts of young people and 18 in 100 (12 to 24) in cross-sectional studies; single studies from 4.5 in 100 (use disorder, US adults aged 50 or more) to 41.1 in 100 (lifetime use disorder, Australian 21-year-olds). No estimate by strength or form exists in these sources.
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias -1: cross-sectional studies with self-reported exposure, five of six rated poor, adjustment ranging from none to frequency and amount, and a narrative review and a pooled prevalence without appraisal. Inconsistency -1: two of six studies, the only direct comparisons of concentrates with herbal cannabis, find no clear difference, and the two reviews disagree on one of them. Indirectness -1: product type as a proxy for THC, screening scales for four of six outcomes, selected samples, and a base rate not split by strength. These downgrades pass the floor, so the certainty is very low. Not downgraded for imprecision or publication bias, and no upgrade (the one gradient mixes strength with frequency of use). Overlapping evidence: three of the four studies that found an association share an author with the review and two of them are described as annual drug surveys, so they are not fully independent replications. Worded 'is associated with' because no study can show direction. The base rate (Leung 2020) is given as a description of the populations sampled; as a description it rests on unappraised surveys pooled across recall periods and DSM versions and would itself be rated low at best.

lines.q: Does stronger cannabis make dependence more likely?
lines.short: Some studies link them: in four of six, people who used stronger cannabis, like skunk, had more signs of a use disorder. None could show cause.
lines.but: All six asked people once and took their word for how strong their cannabis was. Nobody measured THC.
how: A use disorder means use gets hard to control and causes problems. In surveys in richer countries, about 22 in 100 people who'd used cannabis had one.
In one UK survey, each extra day a month of using skunk went with a slightly higher dependence score. Grass and resin showed no link.
The only two studies that compared concentrates with plant cannabis found no clear gap. A later review says how often people use is the surest sign of risk, in any form.
Five of the six were rated poor, and only one allowed for how much people used.

lines.statement: Among 116 adults in Australia who had used ecstasy at least once, surveyed in 2004 through the researchers' acquaintances and their networks and through an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter (Allott & Redman, 2006; 51 in 100 women, mean age 26.5), every respondent reported at least one thing they did to avoid ecstasy's negative side effects, chosen from a list: most often drinking water (96 in 100), limiting the amount of ecstasy (71 in 100), taking breaks or chilling out (62 in 100), a healthy lifestyle (60 in 100) and vitamins or natural products (53 in 100); 30 in 100 took other illegal drugs and 16 in 100 prescription medicines for this. To avoid the comedown in the days after, 4 in 100 had no strategy, and to avoid brain damage, 18 in 100 had none. 41 in 100 had taken pharmaceuticals or natural products before ecstasy ('preloading') and 47 in 100 after it ('postloading'): among those who listed them, half took multivitamins and 41 in 100 took 5-HTP (a building block of serotonin) before, followed by magnesium and fruit or juice, and 46 in 100 took 5-HTP and 44 in 100 multivitamins after; among those who gave reasons, 46 in 100 did it to ease the comedown and 33 in 100 to reduce brain damage. About 39 in 100 had ever tested their pills (61 in 100 never had; editors' calculation), and 53 in 100 had changed how they used ecstasy because of something they disliked about it, most of them by using it less often. Every respondent had also used at least one other substance with ecstasy, most often alcohol (91 in 100 before and 81 in 100 during use) and amphetamines (60 in 100 before and 66 in 100 during). Preloading and postloading were more common among respondents who had used ecstasy more than 50 times (preloading 55 against 30 in 100), among about 30 tests without correction. These figures describe one self-selected sample, not how common the practices are: respondents found through harm-reduction websites may be more interested in harm reduction, the response rate is unknown, the questionnaire was not validated, and how often each strategy was used was not asked. Whether any of these practices lowers harm was not studied: the authors note that the evidence that preloading protects comes only from studies in rodents given injected pre-treatments, and that taking 5-HTP, SSRI antidepressants or St John's wort with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome, which this survey did not examine. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: 116 adults living in Australia who had used ecstasy at least once (51% women; aged 18 to 41, mean 26.5; 79% had used in the past 3 months), surveyed June to December 2004 through the researchers' acquaintances, their networks and an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter
lines.exposure: Ecstasy use, and practices reported before, during and after it: strategies chosen from a list, pill testing, preloading and postloading with pharmaceuticals or natural products, changes in use, other substances used alongside (self-report, lifetime, on an unvalidated questionnaire)
lines.comparator: None for the shares (descriptive); for the correlates, respondents who did and did not preload or postload
lines.outcome: Share of respondents reporting each practice; products taken before or after ecstasy and the reasons given; other substances used with ecstasy
lines.magnitude: Allott & Redman (2006), n = 116: strategies to avoid negative side effects (from a list) drinking water 95.7%, limiting ecstasy 70.7%, breaks or 'chilling out' 62.1%, healthy lifestyle 59.5%, vitamins or natural products 52.6%, other illegal drugs 30.2%, prescription medications 15.5%; no strategy for the comedown 4.4%, for brain damage 18.1%. Pill testing: never 61.2%, rarely 16.4%, a quarter of the time 6%, half 1.7%, three quarters 8.6%, always 6% (ever 38.8%, editors' calculation). Preloaded 41.4%, postloaded 47.4%; preloading products (n = 46) multivitamins 50.0%, 5-HTP 41.3%, magnesium 23.9%, fruit or juice 23.9%; postloading (n = 54) 5-HTP 46.3%, multivitamins 44.4%, fruit or juice 24.1%; reasons (n = 55) to ease the comedown 45.5%, to reduce brain damage 32.7%, to reduce side effects 18.2%. Changed use because of dislikes 53% (61 people: 68.9% less often, 16.4% less per occasion, 13.1% stopped). Used before and during ecstasy: alcohol 91.4% and 81.0%, amphetamines 60.3% and 65.5%. Correlates (about 30 uncorrected tests): preloading with younger age (24.9 against 27.6 years, p = 0.011) and more than 50 occasions (54.7% against 30.2%, p = 0.007); postloading with more than 50 occasions (60.4% against 36.5%, p = 0.01) and monthly use (55.9% against 36.4%, p = 0.036). Editors' calculation: shares near 40–50% carry 95% intervals of about ±9 points.
lines.reasoning: A descriptive survey starts low; rated down for risk of bias (a self-selected sample likely to over-represent interest in harm reduction) and indirectness: very low. The claim gives what this sample reported, not population prevalence, and says nothing about whether any practice works, which the paper did not study. Section 7, findings only, held for the senior author: products are named as respondents reported them, with the authors' caution about serotonin syndrome, and no amounts or timings are given. One reason respondents gave for preloading, to increase the effects of ecstasy (21.8%), is left out under decision p-before-during-after (nothing on making a drug's effects stronger). The paper calls itself the first study of these practices, but its own introduction describes an earlier UK survey (Akram & Galt, 1999), not read. Later surveys of preloading (Copeland et al., 2006; Kelly, 2009) and the rat studies behind it (Sprague et al., 1994) are on the reading list and were not read. Status single study.

lines.q: What do people do before and after ecstasy to lower harm?
lines.short: In a 2004 Australian survey, people who used ecstasy most often said they drank water, took less or took breaks. The survey didn't test whether any of it helps.
lines.but: The 116 people chose to answer, and some came through an ecstasy website. So they may care more about harm reduction than others.
how: From a list of ways to avoid side effects, nearly all picked water, about 7 in 10 taking less, and 6 in 10 taking breaks.
About 4 in 10 had taken vitamins or other products before ecstasy, and nearly half after. Most often these were multivitamins or 5-HTP. Many said they did it to ease the comedown.

The authors say the only evidence that taking things beforehand protects comes from rodents given injections. They warn that 5-HTP, SSRI antidepressants or St John's wort with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome.
